newsitem.title: TURKEY: BOXING-CASH-STRAPPED CHAMPION TODOROV DEFECTS TO TURKEY.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-CASH-STRAPPED CHAMPION TODOROV DEFECTS TO TURKEY.

text.p: World amateur featherweight champion boxer Serafim Todorov said on Friday he had defected to Turkey from Bulgaria after entering on a tourist visa in a move highlighting the fall of the communist sporting empire.
"I came in two days ago -- I walked across the border and the boxing federation picked me up," Todorov, an ethnic Turk, told Reuters in fluent Turkish.

Todorov said he would apply for Turkish citizenship and be known by his Turkish name of Ahmet Sabri. He said he was working on bringing his wife, two children and an uncle -- who had trained him since 1980 -- to Istanbul.
Turkish boxing federation officials said they hoped Todorov would be ready to compete for Turkey in the world championships in Budapest in October.

Unlike triple Olympic weightlifting champion Naim Suleymanoglu, who defected in 1986 to escape Sofia's forced assimilation of ethnic Turks, Todorov said his move was spurred mainly by economic hardship.
He said the Bulgarians were aware of his plans to defect.
"The economic situation is very bad there -- they reduced wages a lot. It was difficult to live," he said. "Half my wages went towards paying my phone bill."
"I wanted to come to Turkey for some time and I had promised the boxing federation that I would come after the Atlanta Olympics."

Todorov, runner-up in the 57-kg class in Atlanta, said he earned 50,000 lev ($21) a month in Bulgaria and lived in a shanty house in the central town of Pestera. Until 1994 he earned a considerably larger sum, he said.
Sudi Topal, executive board chairman of the boxing federation, said Todorov would be given a furnished house in Istanbul and "all his needs will be met".
"The Bulgarians have not directly demanded any money from us," Topal said. "They have realised that they cannot keep hold of such sportsmen if they can only offer such conditions."

The Bulgarians, strapped for cash following the collapse of communism and valuable Soviet sponsorship for sport, had been barely able to hold training camps or direct their boxers' career development, Todorov said.

"They tried to stop me at first -- I first decided I wanted to come in 1989. They tried to frighten me, to bar my way. They are communists, after all. They then wanted money -- they wanted $500,000, then $300,000, then $200,000, but they had to give up on that idea and I was finally able to get a visa," he said.
Turkey handed over a reported $1 million to Bulgaria for Suleymanoglu at a time when relations were strained between the two countries.
With an improvement of bilateral ties and the hardship facing Bulgarian sportsmen, Turkey has since welcomed enough ethnic Bulgarian weightlifters to make an entire new team.
Greece, Georgia and Australia are among other countries to benefit from the addition of impoverished ex-Soviet sportsmen.
